newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr keeps nerve, aided by crosses.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr keeps nerve, aided by crosses.

text.p: The Australian dollar emerged from another burst of profit-taking relatively unscathed Tuesday, and actually extended its steep rally on some major crosses.

The currency was vulnerable given the speed of its two-week, three-cent rise and a second failure to clear US$0.8150 resistance offshore. Japanese investors took the cue to sell and slapped it down to US$0.8080 support, but were themselves caught short by a bounce in US$/yen and buying for a samurai bond.
Sentiment was also aided by a shift in favour against safe haven, low yielding currencies which saw it to a 31-month high on the German mark and a 2-1/2 year peak on the Swiss franc.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar was holding up at US$0.8100/05 from an early US$0.8103/08 and a US$0.8128 high offshore Monday.

Chart watchers said the currency had become dangerously overbought during last week's surge and a correction was both necessary and healthy for the uptrend to a medium term target of US$0.8400/8450. They reckoned the pullback could extend to US$0.8030/50 without endagering the upbeat outlook and it would take a break of US$0.7950 to make them reconsider.
A few more days of consolidation may lie ahead, however, particularly with the U.S. on Thanksgiving holiday Thursday.
On the crosses, it eased to 91.10/20 yen from a four-year high of 91.31, but was still up on Monday's late 90.90/00.
Dealers said Japanese demand, possibly for a dual currency samurai bond, caught the market in a short squeeze and there was talk of a lot more buying to come from this source.

There was some caution in case Wednesday's crucial Bank of Japan Tankan survey of business sentiment proved stronger than expected, an outcome which could threaten to upset the market's cosy assumptions about Japanese interest rates staying low.
That in turn might turn off the tap of Japanese funds which have been pouring into dual currency samurai issues.
A record 308.5 billion yen of such bonds have been launched so far in November and a sizeable chunk have been yen/A$ issues.

But most analysts thought the concerns overdone given that recent signs of strain in Japan's financial system would make it hard for the BOJ to tighten without threatening more bank collapses like last week's suspension of Hanwa Bank.
Indeed, there were rumours today that two regional banks were in financial trouble.
Analysts also looked for fresh demand to emerge from the winter bonus season for workers in Japan with securities houses expected to aggressively market higher yielding samurai issues.

The dollar was also holding sizeable gains on most European crosses as increasing investor confidence in the progress of European Monetary Union reduced the attractiveness of safe, but low yielding, currencies like the mark and Swiss franc.

It was up at a 31-month closing high of 1.2336/47 marks from 1.2274/90 Monday and at 1.0448/53 francs from 1.0284/99, a 2-1/2 year peak. That helped it progress to a new five year high in trade weighted terms of 59.8, up from 59.6 Monday.
There was no domestic data out to offer direction although bulls continued to take comfort in Monday's strong business investment data which augured well for the economy next year.
The next major data would be the September quarter report on enterprise bargain wage deals from the Department of Industrial Relations which were due anytime from Wednesday onwards.
Some of these pay agreements had been running above the Reserve Bank's comfort zone in Q2 and any further pick up in wages growth would lessen the chance of another rate cut, analysts said.
Equally, a slowing in settlements -- which most were actually expecting -- would support talk of an easing in Q1 next year.
